The best in class demonstration of vertical milling was achieved at KEK using 5-axis milling of a X-band accelerating structure, achieving a maximum peak roughness of Ry ≈ 1 μm and a profile accuracy of ± 2.5 μm, with some reports indicating that electropolishing was used [3,7] Images of the proof-of-concept quadrant test piece, a probe-type form measurement demonstrating 5 μm accuracy and a full-scale X-band quadrant are shown below: Figure 9: Ultra-precision milling of high gradient NCRF accelerating structure at KEK [3,7] (Left) Image of reduced scale, proof of concept structure (Center) Profile measurements along structure surface of reduced scale part (Right) Full scale component To achieve these best on class results, KEK contracted the machining effort to Japanese company U- Corporation, which also does high precision machining for aerospace and medical applications [16]. U- corporation was capable of achieving these tight tolerances through a combination of state-of-the-art machining centers (HERMLE-Germany and Yasuda Precision Tools – Japan), tight isothermal temperature control in the machining rooms (±0.5℃) and a vibration dampened, 1-meter thick concrete floor supported by more than 100 piles under the facility. Some of the known current challenges to realizing a welded structure shown are shown in Figure 8. Many of these issues are routinely solved through tooling and manufacturing planning and RF design compromises. For example, undercut features in the cell noses are reduced to sizes that permit manufacturing in conventional 3 axis mills with lollipop undercutting tools and piece part flatness requirements are maintained through clever implementation of tooling to constraint components through the bonding processes. However, the required use of tooling and more involved setups typically results in additional personnel touch time and thus cost increases. This highlights the importance of involving a full engineering and manufacturing team before concluding the RF design process in order to ensure that a production optimized design is realized. Precise machine tools such as vertical milling centers are characterized by high thermal stability and compensation feedback, hydrostatic-dampening, high stiffness, wear-free guideways and drives. Strict adherence to the specified precision also involves the use of controlled waviness of the cutting tools, where the waviness is defined by the amount of deviation from a true circle and is measured from peak to valley (typical range of waviness values is between 0.1 μm and 0.05 μm).
